w: Monks have prayed on this Dartmoor edge since 1018, through a Cistercian abbey, Henry VIII's dissolution in 1539, and three centuries of ruin -- until French Benedictines bought the wreck in 1882 and rebuilt it stone by stone. The new church, finished in 1938, still holds a working monastery today.
s: Dissolved in 1539, rebuilt by the monks who returned.
_facts: Abbey since 1018
Dissolved 1539
French Benedictines bought site 1882, reinstated as abbey 1902
New church built 1907-1938
13 monks as of 2020

w: Danish raiders burned the church in 997; the abbots rebuilt, expanded it in 1285 and again through the 1450s, and then Henry VIII's dissolution in 1539 finished the job for good. All that survives of one of Devon's great Benedictine houses is a refectory, two gateways and a porch.
_facts: Ruined Benedictine abbey
Church destroyed by Danish raiders 997
Rebuilt 1285 and 1457-58
Surrendered 1539
Only refectory, two gateways and a porch remain

w: A small manor house turned fortified ruin on Dartmoor's northeastern edge, a couple of miles from Chagford -- one of the moor's more obscure castle remains, its history thinner on record than most of the region's better-documented ruins.
s: An obscure castle ruin on Dartmoor's edge.
_facts: Manor house of the manor of Gidleigh
NE edge of Dartmoor, ~2 miles NW of Chagford

w: This tor sits on private land, and since 2003 its owner has banned the public from climbing it -- a closure that has provoked protests and mass trespasses by hikers and climbers who consider the moor's open-access tradition non-negotiable. The standoff, over one of Dartmoor's best-known rock stacks, continues.
_facts: Tor on Dartmoor
Private land, public access banned since 2003
Caused protests and mass trespass by hikers and climbers

w: Named for Cut Lane, the old drovers' track that once cut livestock through the fen between the Dart and Tavy valleys, this 603m summit sits deep in a military training area, reachable only at certain times and after a slog through wet peat hags. The view from the top is called among Dartmoor's best.
_facts: 603m, joint third-highest peak in Dartmoor
Within military training area, restricted access
~1.5hr walk from Postbridge
Named after drovers' track Cut Lane
Panoramic views 'among the best Dartmoor offers'

w: Built after a Norman revolt in 1068, this motte-and-bailey grew into a hunting lodge for the Earls of Devon. Wars of the Roses confiscations followed, and after Henry Courtenay's execution under Henry VIII the castle was left to rot -- ruins picturesque enough to draw the painter Turner two centuries on.
s: Devon's largest castle, later painted by Turner.
_facts: Built 1068-1086 by Baldwin FitzGilbert
Redeveloped as luxury hunting lodge by the Courtenays
Confiscated repeatedly during Wars of the Roses
Abandoned after Henry Courtenay's execution
Painted by J.M.W. Turner, now English Heritage

w: A Tudor mansion raised inside an older castle's walls by the Pomeroy family, sold off in 1547 to the Duke of Somerset's line when the money ran out, then abandoned by the late 17th century. Two centuries of picturesque decay later, it's one of Devon's most-visited ruins -- and reputedly its most haunted.
_facts: Tudor mansion built within earlier castle walls
Sold to Edward Seymour, Duke of Somerset, 1547
Abandoned late 17th century
Reputation for being haunted
Excavated 1980-1996

w: Built in 1195 as a prison and courtroom enforcing the laws of Dartmoor's Forest and its tin-mining stannaries, this stone tower ran courts for the Duchy of Cornwall into the 19th century -- and earned a longstanding, bad reputation for the harsh injustice meted out inside it.
s: A castle known for injustice, not defense.
_facts: Stone tower built 1195, used as prison and court
Administered Forest of Dartmoor and stannary law
Passed to Duchy of Cornwall 1342
Used until 19th century
Bad reputation for injustice by the 14th century

w: One of England's best-preserved Norman motte-and-bailey castles, raised as the seat of the feudal barony of Totnes soon after 1066. The stone keep and curtain wall standing today were rebuilt around the 14th century, still commanding the River Dart from atop their earthen mound.
_facts: One of best-preserved Norman motte-and-bailey castles in England
Caput of feudal barony of Totnes after 1066
Surviving keep and curtain wall date from 14th century

w: A 700-year-old house on the edge of the moor with two Elizabethan sea-dog owners: raised up by Sir Richard Grenville, then bought by Sir Francis Drake himself. Now in National Trust hands, it's one of the more improbable retirement addresses for the man who circumnavigated the globe.
_facts: Grade I listed 700-year-old house
Connections to Sir Richard Grenville and Sir Francis Drake
Owned by the National Trust

w: This 33-acre zoo on Dartmoor's southwestern edge closed under its founder in 2006, only for journalist Benjamin Mee to buy it months later and write a book about the gamble -- We Bought a Zoo -- that became a 2011 film of the same name. It now runs as a conservation and education charity.
s: The real zoo behind 'We Bought a Zoo'.
_facts: 33-acre zoo near Sparkwell, opened 1968
Closed 2006, bought by Benjamin Mee same year
Basis for the book and 2011 film We Bought a Zoo
Became conservation charity 2014

w: A heavily weathered granite outcrop just off the road between Bovey Tracey and Widecombe, its rocks carved into strange shapes by centuries of moorland weather. At its foot lie the stone ruins of a deserted medieval village, English Heritage-managed, with older prehistoric remains scattered close by.
s: A tor overlooking a lost medieval village.
_facts: Heavily weathered granite tor
Includes ruins of a deserted medieval village
Prehistoric stone works nearby
Managed by Dartmoor National Park Authority for English Heritage

w: Above the River Walkham near Princetown sits one of Dartmoor's grandest hills, its summit hollowed by a strange rock basin known as the Devil's Frying Pan. The Duchy of Cornwall leases this ground to the army for live firing -- and unexploded munitions have killed and injured walkers who strayed off the path.
s: The Devil's Frying Pan, and live ordnance.
_facts: One of the grandest hills in Devon
Rock basin called the Devil's Frying Pan
Land leased to the army
Deaths/injuries from unexploded munitions

w: Known as the 'Cathedral of the Moor' for a 120-foot tower absurdly large for so small a village, this granite church was mid-service in 1638 when ball lightning tore through it, killing four of roughly 300 worshippers -- locals blamed a visit from the Devil himself. Its roof bosses still carry the tinners' three hares.
s: Struck by the Devil, or so the story goes.
_facts: Nicknamed Cathedral of the Moor for its 120ft tower
Built 14th century, Grade I listed
Struck by ball lightning during the Great Thunderstorm of 1638, 4 killed
Local legend blamed the Devil
Roof bosses carry the Tinners' Rabbits emblem
